title: FA/27/2021 of LOVISH GOEL Vs YASHA AGARWAL

paras.text:
IN THE HIGH COURT OF UTTARAKHAND
AT NAINITAL
THE HON'BLE THE CHIEF JUSTICE SRI RAGHVENDRA SINGH CHAUHAN
AND
THE HON'BLE SRI JUSTICE ALOK KUMAR VERMA
12th APRIL, 2021
FIRST APPEAL NO.27 of 2021
Between:
Lovish Goel. ...Appellant
Versus
Smt. Yasha Agarwal. ...Respondent
Counsel for the
appellant.
: Mr. Navneet Kaushik.
The Court made the following:
JUDGMENT: (per Hon'ble Sri Justice Alok Kumar Verma)

This Appeal has been filed under Section 19 of
the Family Courts Act, 1984 against the order dated
04.03.2021, passed by the learned Additional Judge,
Family Court, Roorkee, District Haridwar in Original Suit
No.227 of 2019, "Lovish Goel vs. Smt. Yasha Agarwal",
whereby, the learned trial court, while deciding the
preliminary issue on the ground of the territorial
jurisdiction, came to the conclusion that it did not have

2
territorial jurisdiction to entertain the petition, filed
under Section 13 (1) (i-a) of the Hindu Marriage Act,
1955 (hereinafter referred to as, 'the Act').
2. Heard Mr. Navneet Kaushik, the learned
counsel for the appellant.
3. According to the appellant, the appellant and
the respondent are Hindus. They were married on
18.04.2017 at Muzaffarnagar (Uttar Pradesh) in
accordance with the Hindu rites. After marriage, the
couple went to Gurgaon on 25.06.2017 and resided
there till 05.06.2018. The appellant and the respondent
have never resided together at any place thereafter. The
respondent came to Roorkee (appellant's residence) with
her parents on 25.08.2018. However, she was not ready
to live in Roorkee and on the same night i.e. on
25.08.2018, she went back to Muzaffarnagar (her
parental house) with her parents.
4. Mr. Navneet Kaushik, the learned counsel for
the appellant submitted that since the appellant and the
respondent were together at Roorkee on 25.08.2018,
the Family Court at Roorkee had territorial jurisdiction to
entertain his petition, filed under Section 13 (1) (i-a) of
the Act. He further argued that earlier, the appellant had
filed a petition (No.417 of 2018) against the respondent
under Section 9 of the Act. In that petition, filed under

3
Section 9 of the Act, the appellant had taken the
identical pleadings regarding the territorial jurisdiction
and the very court i.e. the Additional Family Court,
Roorkee, decided and allowed the said petition of the
appellant, filed under Section 9 of the Act, ex-parte on
27.03.2019. The learned counsel for the appellant
further submitted that in these circumstances, the
learned trial court should decide the present matter on
merits.
5. Section 19 of the Act, deals with territorial
jurisdiction of the petitions, filed under the Act. Section
19 of the Act is reproduced as under:-
"19. Court to which petition shall be
presented. - (1) Every petition under this Act shall
be presented to the district court within the local
limits of whose ordinary original civil jurisdiction-
(i) the marriage was solemnized, or
(ii) the respondent, at the time of the
presentation of the petition resides, or
(iii) the parties to the marriage last resided
together, or
(iii-a) in case the wife is the petitioner,
where she is residing on the date of
presentation of the petition, or

4
(iv) the petitioner is residing at the time of
the presentation of the petition, in a case
where the respondent is, at that time,
residing outside the territories to which this
Act extends, or has not been heard of as
being alive for a period of seven years or
more by those persons who would naturally
have heard of him if he were alive."
6. Section 19 of the Act regulates the venue and
lays down the territorial limits for the purpose of
jurisdiction. It is the "district court" as defined in Section
3 (b) of the Act that has jurisdiction to entertain and try
matters arising under the Act. The Family Courts Act,
1984 has been enacted to provide for the establishment
of Family Courts with a view to promote conciliation in,
and secure speedy settlement of, disputes relating to
marriage and family affairs and for matters connected
therewith. Therefore, now, the "district court" as defined
under Section 3 (b) of the Act, shall be deemed to have
been substituted by the words "Family Court" as per
Section 7 of the Family Courts Act, 1984.
7. According to Section 19 of the Act, one is the
territorial jurisdiction of a Family Court within which the
marriage was solemnized. The second relates to the
place of residence of the respondent at the time of the

5
presentation of the petition. The third relates to the
place where the parties to the marriage last resided
together.
8. It is not the case of the appellant that the
marriage was solemnized at Roorkee or at the time of
the presentation of his petition, under Section 13 (1) (i-a) of the Act, the respondent was residing at Roorkee.
According to the appellant, the respondent came to
Roorkee with her parents on 25.08.2018. Therefore, the
appellant and the respondent last resided together at
Roorkee.
9. The expression "resided" has not been defined
in the Act. According to the Webster Dictionary "to
reside" means "to dwell permanently or for any length of
time." Black's Law Dictionary defines "reside" as to settle
oneself or a thing in a place, to be stationed, to remain
or stay, to dwell permanently or continuously. Therefore,
"last resided" does not mean the temporary or casual
stay for the purpose of obtaining divorce.
10. In Jeewanti Pandey vs. Kishan Chandra
Pandey, (1981) 4 SCC 517, the Hon'ble Supreme
Court has observed that in order to give jurisdiction on
the ground of "last resided" something more than a
temporary stay is required. In its ordinary sense
"residence" is more or less of a permanent character.

6
11. It should be noted that the petition No.417 of
2018, "Lovish Goel vs. Smt. Yasha Agarwal", filed under
Section 9 of the Act, was allowed ex-parte by the
learned Additional Family Court, Roorkee, District
Haridwar on 27.03.2019, whereas, in the present
matter, the respondent appeared before the Additional
Family Court, Roorkee and filed her written statement.
She raised objections regarding the territorial jurisdiction
of the Additional Family Court, Roorkee at the initial
stage. The said objection has been raised by the
respondent at the earliest possible opportunity and
before settlement of issues. When a preliminary issue is
raised in a case which affects the maintainability of a
petition on the ground of the territorial jurisdiction, it
should ordinarily be decided at an earliest stage. Where
the question of returning the petition for want of
territorial jurisdiction is involved, it is better that it
should be decided first. An issue regarding the territorial
jurisdiction, involving question of law, should be tried as
a preliminary issue and it is settled law that once the
court holds that it has no jurisdiction in the matter, it
should not consider the merits of the matter.
12. From the aforesaid discussions, the
submissions, raised by the learned counsel for the
appellant, cannot be accepted. The impugned order of
the learned trial court is perfectly sustainable under law

7
and no good grounds have been made out to interfere
with the impugned order dated 04.03.2021, passed by
the learned Additional Judge, Family Court, Roorkee,
District Haridwar. The instant appeal sans merits and is
dismissed at the admission stage.
